description: Certificate_Store::certificate_known() calls find_cert(DN, SKI) and returns true if any result exists, discarding the returned object instead of comparing it to the input certificate. DN and SKI are non-cryptographic, attacker-chosen fields (and find_cert falls back to DN-only when SKI is absent). The path builder (x509path.cpp:691) calls this on the attacker-supplied end-entity cert and, on a match, emits a length-1 chain containing only the attacker's cert. All downstream checks (signature, CA constraint, hostname, revocation, name constraints) then validate the attacker's cert against itself, so the real root's public key is never consulted. A MITM attacker can therefore forge a certificate for any hostname that any default Botan TLS client will accept.
reproduction: 1. Pick any root CA in the victim's trust store.
2. Copy its Subject DN and SubjectKeyIdentifier into a new certificate (or omit SKI to collide on DN alone).
3. Set SAN=DNS:<target-hostname> and self-sign with a fresh keypair.
4. Present this certificate as the server cert from a MITM position.
5. Botan's path builder marks it as a known trust anchor, builds a length-1 chain, and all checks (self-signature, CA, hostname, revocation, name constraints) pass against the attacker's own cert.
technical_details:
Hi Jack --

I'm a security researcher at Anthropic. I believe I've found a

certificate-verification bypass in Botan's X.509 path validator that

lets a network attacker forge a certificate that any default Botan TLS

client accepts for any hostname. I've attached a demo that crafts a

self-signed cert with a copied DN+SKI and connects with Botan's own

cert_verify tool; OpenSSL rejects the same chain.

(Up-front disclosure: an LLM found this bug. I validated it myself

against Botan HEAD. I stand by this report personally and vouch for

its correctness.)

The bug is in Certificate_Store::certificate_known():

    // src/lib/x509/certstor.h:80-82

    bool certificate_known(const X509_Certificate& cert) const {

       return find_cert(cert.subject_dn(), cert.subject_key_id()).has_value();

    }

The method answers the question "does the store contain some cert with

this DN+SKI?" rather than the correct question "does the store contain

*this* cert?". It discards the certificate that find_cert() returns

and only checks .has_value(). DN and SKI are both non-cryptographic

fields the certificate holder chooses freely---RFC 5280 section

4.2.1.2 describes SKI as a means "to facilitate certification path

construction" and states that "applications are not required to verify

that key identifiers match when performing certification path

validation."

find_cert() itself (certstor.cpp:57-75) makes this worse by falling back

to DN-only when the caller's SKI is empty:

    if(!key_id.empty()) {

       const std::vector<uint8_t>& skid = cert.subject_key_id();

       if(!skid.empty() && skid != key_id) { continue; }

    }

    if(cert.subject_dn() == subject_dn) { return cert; }

So an attacker who omits the SKI extension entirely collides on DN

alone.

The consuming site is the path builder:

    // src/lib/x509/x509path.cpp:691-693

    auto cert_in_any_trusted_store = [&](const X509_Certificate& cert) {

       return std::ranges::any_of(trusted_certstores,

          [&](const Certificate_Store* store) {

              return store->certificate_known(cert); });

    };

This lambda is called on the end-entity certificate -- the first cert

in the server-supplied chain. Every every byte of this certificate is,

by construction, attacker-controlled. Once it returns true, the DFS

path builder emits a length-1 chain of just the attacker's cert as a

valid path.

All of the downstream check then passes, because the attacker's cert is

validated against itself:

  - Signature verification: at_trust_anchor=true so issuer=cert_path[0]

    (the attacker's cert). Verifies attacker's self-signature against

    attacker's own public key. Passes.

  - CA constraint: is_end_entity_trust_anchor=true for length-1 chains,

    so the check short-circuits.

  - Hostname: checked against cert_path[0]'s SAN -- which the attacker

    set to the target hostname.

  - Revocation: the trust-anchor loop runs chain_status.size()-1

    iterations; for size 1 that's zero.

  - Name constraints: issuer is the attacker's own cert; the real root's

    constraints are never loaded.

The real trust anchor's public key is never read into memory during

validation.

The attack, then, is trivial:

  1. Pick any root CA in the victim's trust store (Mozilla bundle,

     system store -- all public).

  2. Copy its Subject DN and SubjectKeyIdentifier into a new cert.

  3. Set SAN=DNS:target-hostname, self-sign with a fresh keypair.

  4. Present as the server certificate from a MITM position.

Running the attached PoC against Botan HEAD (70da513, 2026-03-26):

    $ ./botan cert_verify forged_ee.pem trust_anchor.pem

    Certificate passes validation checks

    $ openssl verify -CAfile trust_anchor.pem forged_ee.pem

    CN = Acme Corporate Root CA, O = Acme Corp

    error 18 at 0 depth lookup: self-signed certificate

    error forged_ee.pem: verification failed

The certificates share DN and SKI but have completely different keys:

    Trust anchor pubkey SHA-256:  1367c23ab13fe3a1fc498837...

    Forged EE    pubkey SHA-256:  7fe67b5cad53213f79bd1a7d...

The fix is one line. X509_Certificate::operator== already compares

signature, signature algorithm, and tbs bytes (x509cert.cpp:696-699):

    bool certificate_known(const X509_Certificate& cert) const {

       auto found = find_cert(cert.subject_dn(), cert.subject_key_id());

       return found.has_value() && (*found == cert);

    }

Alternatively, build_all_certificate_paths could place the store's

certificate object into the chain rather than the attacker-supplied one,

so downstream checks use the trusted public key. Either closes the hole;

the certificate_known() change is minimal. Patch attached.

The method is non-virtual and inherited unchanged by every

Certificate_Store backend (In_Memory, Flatfile, System, Windows, MacOS,

In_SQL), so the fix at the base class covers all of them.

Please let me know if you have any questions.

Nicholas

You can reproduce this on any machine with Botan built:

  # Build Botan (if needed)

  git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/randombit/botan.git

  cd botan && python3 configure.py --build-targets=static,cli && make -j

  # Generate the PoC certs (or use the attached .pem files)

  bash gen_certs.sh

  # Botan accepts the forged cert

  ./botan cert_verify forged_ee.pem trust_anchor.pem

  # -> Certificate passes validation checks

  # OpenSSL correctly rejects it

  openssl verify -CAfile trust_anchor.pem forged_ee.pem

  # -> error 18 at 0 depth lookup: self-signed certificate

  # Control: unrelated DN is correctly rejected by Botan too

  ./botan cert_verify control_ee.pem trust_anchor.pem

  # -> Certificate did not validate - Cannot establish trust
title: [security] certificate_known(): Complete x509 bypass
